questions.question: Why does Context struggle as a store for frequently-changing, widely-read state?
options: Context can only hold strings and numbers
Every consumer of a Context re-renders whenever the Provider's value changes, even if it only reads one field
Context requires a separate npm package to work
Context values cannot be updated after the Provider mounts
questions.explanation: A Context Provider re-render fans out to every consumer, regardless of which part of the value object a given consumer actually reads.

questions.question: What is a key reason libraries like Zustand avoid Context's re-render fan-out problem?
options: They don't use React state internally at all
Components subscribe only to the specific slice of the store they read, so unrelated changes don't re-render them
They disable re-renders globally for the whole app
They only work with class components
questions.explanation: Stores like Zustand let a component select just the slice it needs (e.g. `state => state.items.length`), so it only re-renders when that specific slice changes.

questions.question: According to the lesson's decision order, what should you try before reaching for Context or a global store?
options: Immediately install Redux Toolkit for any shared value
Colocate state locally in the component that needs it, lifting it only as high as actual consumers require
Convert all components to class components
questions.explanation: The recommended default is local state, lifted only as far as necessary — global state is reached for only once that stops being sufficient.

questions.question: Pairing Context with `useReducer` gives you a pattern most similar to:
options: A lightweight, dependency-free version of Redux's dispatch-action-reducer model
questions.explanation: Dispatching actions to a centralized reducer, exposed via Context, mirrors Redux's core pattern without adding an external library.
